title: Al-Mu'nisa
intro: This is the poem known as al-Mu'nisa, “the companion”: Dawud al-Antaki, in Tazyin al-Aswaq, calls it the longest poem the Majnun recited and kept reciting, and passes on a report that he knew it by heart, unlike his other poems, and recited it whenever he was alone. Al-Aghani tells of Nawfal ibn Musahiq meeting the Majnun, a handsome man grown pale, and hearing this poem from him; it calls the poem “among his most famous”, and reports that when he spoke its line “He decreed her for another and tried me with love for her”, his mind was taken from him. It moves from the memory of Layla and her fire glimpsed far off at night, through complaints against fate and the talebearers, a love that turns him towards her even in prayer and the doves of the valley of Nu'man, to his friends bringing his bier and shroud. The early authorities doubted the Majnun himself (al-Aghani has al-Asma'i call him, in one report, a name the transmitters made up, and in others a man touched rather than mad, to whom more verse was credited than he composed; it has al-Jahiz say that every anonymous poem about a Layla was credited to him, and men like Nawfal say they saw him), and the text varies as much: 71 lines in the printed diwan of Abu Bakr al-Walibi's recension, 83 in another order in the manuscript Abd al-Sattar Farraj copied. The reciter follows al-Walibi's order, leaves out one line, and closes with a line that Farraj prints as the end of another poem on the same rhyme.

translation: I remembered Layla and the years gone by,
and days when we feared no one would forbid our play.
1.sharh: The poem opens on memory: Layla, and the years of youth when the two of them could enjoy themselves with no one to stop them. Remembering her and remembering that freer time are one and the same.

translation: And many a day, long as a spear's shadow, I made short
with Layla; it drew me into play, though I was no idler.
2.sharh: One long day, long as a spear's shadow, flew by at Layla's side and drew him into play, though play was never his habit. Its hours were as long as ever; her company made them feel short.

translation: At Thamdin Layla's fire came into sight, as my companions
at Dhat al-Ghada drove the swift camels on.
3.sharh: Travelling by night with his companions, he sees a fire far off at Thamdin, where Layla's people are camped. In the desert a fire marks a camp, so to see her fire is to know where she is.

translation: The keenest-eyed of the party said: “I glimpsed a star
rising alone in the dark of night, to the south.”
4.sharh: His companion, the sharpest-eyed among them, takes the light for a star: a single point in the southern sky, the quarter Arabs called Yemen's. The fire is so far off and so high that it passes for a star.

translation: I told him: “No, it is Layla's fire, kindled
on a height; its light climbed and showed itself to me.”
5.sharh: He corrects his friend: the light is not a star but Layla's fire, lit on high ground so that its glow rises and reaches him across the dark. What the friend takes for a star, the lover knows for hers.

translation: If only the party's camels had not crossed the Ghada,
and the Ghada had walked beside the camels for nights.
6.sharh: He wishes the caravan had never left the ghada country where Layla's fire burned, or, impossibly, that the land itself could travel along with them. The place is dear to him only because it is hers.

translation: O Layla, how many pressing needs I carry,
but coming to you at night, I forget what they are.
7.sharh: He comes to her with much to say and much to ask, but at the sight of her by night he forgets every word of it. Her presence empties his mind of everything he had prepared.

translation: My two friends, unless you weep for me, I will seek
a friend to weep for me when my tears run dry.
8.sharh: If his two companions will not share his grief, he will find another friend: one who will weep in his place once his own tears have run out. A true friend carries the grief he can no longer carry.

translation: I climb no hilltop but out of longing,
and recite no poem but as a cure.
9.sharh: He climbs high ground only to look towards Layla's country, and makes verses only to soothe his pain, not for pleasure. Al-Aghani says he spoke these lines to a man of Qushayr who found him singing and asked whether Layla did not keep him from song.

translation: God may yet bring together two who were scattered,
after each was sure beyond all doubt they would never meet.
10.sharh: He consoles himself with hope: God sometimes reunites two people long after both have given up any thought of meeting again. Grammarians quote the second half for its emphatic construction, literally “they think all the thinking”.

translation: God curse the people who say: “We have found
that the long passage of time cures love.”
11.sharh: He curses those who claim that time heals love. His own long years of suffering prove them wrong: time has passed, and he is no nearer to a cure than he was at the start.

translation: I knew Layla when she still wore a little girl's shift,
driving the herds back to us at evening.
12.sharh: His memory of her reaches back to her childhood, when she was a small girl in a child's shift who brought the flocks home at dusk. His love is as old as her girlhood.

translation: Layla's sons grew up, and her son's sons grew up,
and what ties me to Layla stays in my heart unchanged.
13.sharh: Years go by: her sons grow to manhood, then her grandsons, and she becomes a grandmother. His attachment has not aged at all; it sits in his heart exactly as it did at the start.

translation: Whenever we sit together somewhere we delight in,
they spread tales of us till I tire of my place.
14.sharh: Whenever he and Layla find a pleasant hour together, the talebearers start whispering about them, until the place grows hateful to him and he gets up and leaves. Gossip spoils even their best moments.

translation: God send rain on Layla's neighbours, carried far away
by the journey, to where they have camped at al-Matali.
15.sharh: He prays for rain on the women of Layla's camp, now moved far off to al-Matali. Praying for rain on a place and its people was the Arabs' blessing, since rain meant pasture and life; blessing her neighbours is a way of blessing her.

translation: Neither want nor wealth has made me forget Layla,
nor repentance, even when I clung to the mosque's pillars.
16.sharh: Nothing has made him forget her: not poverty, not riches, not even turning to God so earnestly that he clung to the columns of the mosque. Every remedy that makes men forget has failed.

translation: nor women who painted an old, heavy-waisted woman
to look like Layla, then put her in my way.
17.sharh: Nor did the women's trick work: they made up a stout, ageing woman to pass for Layla and paraded her before him, hoping she would console him. No one else can stand in for Layla.

translation: My two friends, no, by God, I have no say in what
God decreed for Layla, or what He decreed for me.
18.sharh: He swears he is powerless before God's decree: she was destined for another man, and he was destined to love her. Al-Aghani reports that when he spoke this line and the next, he lost his mind.

translation: He decreed her for another and tried me with love for her;
why did He not try me with anything but Layla?
19.sharh: God gave Layla to another man and made love of her the trial he must bear; he asks why it could not have been any other trial. Al-Aghani tells that a voice reproached him that night for resenting God's decree, and his mind was taken from him.

translation: You two told me Tayma is where Layla camps
when summer has cast its anchors.
20.sharh: His friends had told him that Layla's people spend the summer at Tayma, so he waited for summer to bring her near. Summer “casting its anchors” means settling in, as a ship does when it anchors.

translation: Now the summer months have passed us by;
why does parting fling Layla to such distant places?
21.sharh: Summer has come and gone and he has not met her at Tayma as he was told. He asks why separation keeps hurling her farther away, as if parting were an archer and Layla its arrow.

translation: If a talebearer lived in al-Yamama
and I in farthest Hadramawt, he would find his way to me.
22.sharh: The slanderers are relentless: put half of Arabia between them, one in al-Yamama in the centre and he in Hadramawt in the far south, and the slanderer would still track him down to make mischief.

translation: What do they gain, may God never mend their lot,
when Layla cuts the ropes that tie me to her?
23.sharh: He asks what the slanderers gain when Layla, turned by their tales, cuts the ties of love between them, and curses them in the same breath. They do harm for its own sake, with nothing to gain from it.

translation: I used to master my love for Layla, but making
and unmaking resolve wore me down until it mastered me.
24.sharh: At first he mastered his love. But he kept resolving to forget her and then breaking his resolve, like a rope twisted and untwisted, until love mastered him. The same verb, “to be above”, serves both: he was above his love, then it was above him.

translation: Lord, make the love between her and me even,
so that it comes out square, neither against me nor for me.
25.sharh: He asks God to balance their love, so that she loves him exactly as he loves her. He wants no advantage, only fairness: an even account, with nothing owed on either side.

translation: The star that guides travellers never rose,
nor the dawn, without stirring up her memory in me.
26.sharh: Night journeys are steered by a star and end at dawn, and both bring Layla back to his mind. The traveller's whole night, from the guiding star to sunrise, is full of her.

translation: nor did I go a mile from Damascus, nor did Suhayl
rise for the people of Syria, but the thought of her rose for me.
27.sharh: Even a mile out of Damascus, the thought of her comes to him. Suhayl rises for the people of Syria as a star; for him it brings Layla to mind, perhaps because her country lies to the south, where it rises.

translation: No woman who shares her name was ever named before me
without my tears soaking my cloak.
28.sharh: Even another woman called Layla is enough: whenever the name is spoken in front of him he weeps until his cloak is wet. The name alone carries all his grief.

translation: No south wind ever blew from her country by night
but I spent the night bent towards the wind.
29.sharh: The south wind comes from Layla's country, so when it blows at night he spends the night leaning into it, as if to catch something of her on it. The wind from her land is her messenger.

translation: If you keep Layla from me and fence her country
against me, you will never fence the rhymes against me.
30.sharh: He defies her family: they can bar him from her and close her land to him, but they cannot stop his poems about her. Verse goes where he cannot, and no guard can keep it out.

translation: I swear before God that I love her:
that much she has from me: what have I from her?
31.sharh: He calls God to witness his love: that much she can be sure of from him. Then comes the question that torments him: what, if anything, does she feel for him in return.

translation: God decreed her kindness for another,
and for me He decreed longing and passion.
32.sharh: God has divided the shares: her kindness and company go to another man, her husband, while his own share is longing and the torment of love. He states it as a decree he has no power to change.

translation: What I hoped for from you, Umm Malik,
has turned my hair white and driven my heart wild.
33.sharh: He speaks to Layla by her kunya, Umm Malik. The hope he pinned on her, never fulfilled, has turned his hair white and driven his heart wild. Both the grey and the madness are the work of hoping for her.

translation: I count the nights, one night after another,
I who lived a lifetime never counting the nights.
34.sharh: Separation has turned him into a man who counts nights, each one long and empty. Once, when Layla was near, time passed and he never thought to count it.

translation: I slip out from among the tents, hoping
to talk to my heart of you alone in the night.
35.sharh: He leaves the camp at night for open ground, so that he can be alone and speak to himself about her. Solitude is the only company he wants, because it lets him think of Layla.

translation: When I pray, I find I have turned my face
towards her, though the direction of prayer lies behind me.
36.sharh: Love has taken over even his prayer: he finds himself facing Layla's land when he stands to pray, with the direction of Mecca at his back. The next line hastens to deny any idolatry.

translation: It is not that I worship another, but love of her
and the weight of my grief have defeated the healer.
37.sharh: He denies any idolatry in turning towards her: it is sickness, not worship. Her love and the depth of his pain are a disease that no physician has been able to cure.

translation: Of all names I love those that match hers,
or resemble it, or come close to it.
38.sharh: His love spills over onto anything that recalls her, even names: the same name, a similar one, one that only sounds near it. It is the other side of line 28, where the same name makes him weep.

translation: My two friends, Layla is the greatest of my needs and hopes:
who will bring me Layla, or bring me to her?
39.sharh: Layla is the first and largest of all his wishes. He asks who might unite them, whether by bringing her to him or taking him to her; how it happens does not matter, only that it does.

translation: By my life, dove of al-Aqiq, you have made me weep,
and made eyes already weeping weep.
40.sharh: The cooing of a dove in the valley of al-Aqiq moves him to tears, and moves every eye that is used to weeping. To a lover, a dove's call sounds like mourning.

translation: My two friends, what can I hope from life now
that I see my heart's want sold, and not bought for me?
41.sharh: His “want” is Layla, given in marriage to another man for a bride-price: sold, as he puts it, but not to him. With that, life holds nothing more for him to hope for.

translation: Layla does the wrong, then claims
I have forgotten her, though no one can miss what ails me.
42.sharh: She is the one at fault, staying away and turning cold, yet she accuses him of having got over her. Everyone else can see his condition plainly; only she pretends not to.

translation: I have never seen two like us, two friends in longing,
more true to each other in spite of their enemies.
43.sharh: He and Layla, joined by love, are the most loyal pair he has ever seen, their bond unbroken despite all that enemies and talebearers have done. The poem swings between doubt of her love and certainty of it.

translation: Two friends with no hope of meeting, while we see
no other two friends but hope to meet.
44.sharh: Every other pair of lovers lives on the hope of meeting; he and Layla alone have given that hope up, and love each other all the same. Theirs is a love without expectation.

translation: I am too shy of you to let my wishes offer
your love, or to let you come to me in my wishes.
45.sharh: His reverence for her goes so far that he is ashamed even to wish for her love, or to let her into his daydreams. Even imagining her feels like taking a liberty.

translation: People say: “Perhaps the Majnun of Amir
is trying to forget.” I said: “How, with what I have?”
46.sharh: People suppose the madman of the tribe of Amir is trying to get over Layla; he answers that nothing could cure what he carries. Al-Aghani reports al-Utbi's claim that the name Majnun came from this very line.

translation: Despair, or the sickness of love-madness, has struck me:
keep away from me, lest what I have takes you too.
47.sharh: He warns whoever comes near him to keep his distance, as from a contagious illness. Despair and the madness of love are a sickness, and he would not wish his on anyone.

translation: If time drags on, Umm Malik, then leave
the deadly fates and me to settle our affair.
48.sharh: If the separation goes on much longer, he says, let death and him settle matters between them. The phrase is an idiom of letting go: leave me to it. Only death will end his torment.

translation: When my eye takes your eye for kohl, it stays well,
and clears a flood of sorrow from my heart.
49.sharh: Seeing her is like kohl for his eyes, the black salve applied to the eyelids. One look keeps his eye well and lifts the grief that has drowned his heart.

translation: You are the one who, if you wish, makes me wretched,
and the one who, if you wish, sets my heart at ease.
50.sharh: His happiness and his misery are both in her hands. A word from her can ruin his life or give him peace, and he admits that she alone holds that power.

translation: And you are the one whose leavings of me, wasted, no friend
or enemy can see without pitying me.
51.sharh: Love of her has worn him down to a thin remnant of himself. Anyone who sees what she has left of him, friend or enemy, feels sorry for him.

translation: When I ride through open country, I find myself
coaxing my saddle to lean my way.
52.sharh: Even on the road his body bends towards her: he catches himself shifting his saddle so that it leans the way his heart pulls. The next line says which way that is.

translation: Rightward, if she is to the right; and if she is
to the left, love tugs me over to my left.
53.sharh: His body follows where she is: if her country lies to his right he leans right, if to his left, love drags him left. He cannot ride straight, wherever she may be.

translation: I wrap myself for sleep though I am not drowsy,
hoping a phantom of you might meet my own.
54.sharh: He lies down and covers himself without feeling sleepy, only because in sleep her phantom might come and meet his. Dreams are the one place where their meeting is still possible.

translation: She is magic, except that magic has its spell to undo it,
and for her I can never find one who knows the spell.
55.sharh: Layla bewitches him like sorcery, only worse: every spell can be broken by a counter-charm, while for her no charmer exists. Her hold on him has no cure.

translation: When we set out by night and you are ahead of us,
the thought of you is guide enough for our camels.
56.sharh: When their night journey leads towards Layla, they need no star or pathfinder: the thought of her is enough to steer the camels. Longing knows the way better than any guide.

translation: The fire of my longing flared up in my heart,
and now its blaze burns fierce in my heart.
57.sharh: His longing is a fire lit in his heart that has grown into a steady, fierce blaze. The heart is named in both halves: the fire starts there and stays there.

translation: You riders of Yemen, turn aside
to us: our love has become Yemeni too.
58.sharh: He calls on a party of Yemeni riders to stop for him, since his beloved now lives in their direction. They may carry news of her, or let him ride with them.

translation: I ask you: has Nu'man run with floodwater since we left?
How dear to us is the hollow of Nu'man, of all valleys.
59.sharh: He asks the travellers whether rain has made the valley of Nu'man flow since he left, a question that means: is the land green and its people well? Then he cannot help exclaiming how dear the valley is to him.

translation: You two doves of the hollow of Nu'man, you stirred
my love against me when you sang to me.
60.sharh: Two doves cooing in the valley of Nu'man reawaken his passion. Their song is innocent, but it turns his own love against him; to a lover, birds calling to each other are a reminder of what he lacks.

translation: You made me weep among my companions; I would not
have minded my tears if I had been alone.
61.sharh: The doves bring on his tears in front of his friends, and it is the embarrassment that hurts. Alone, he would have let the tears flow without a second thought.

translation: And you two turtle-doves, answer each other
with your songs, then coo, and keep my mind off it.
62.sharh: Now he asks the birds to go on singing, answering each other, so that their cooing might distract and console him. The song that made him weep is also the only comfort he has.

translation: If you two are stirred to song, or wish
to reach the ruins at al-Ghada, then follow me.
63.sharh: He invites the doves to come along: if they feel like singing, or want to see the abandoned camp at al-Ghada, they can follow him there. He is heading back to where Layla's people once camped.

translation: I wish I knew what Layla and I are to each other,
and what youthful love is to me, now grey hair covers me.
64.sharh: He wonders at himself: what business does an ageing man have with Layla and with the passions of youth? He has grown too old for love, but love has not let him go.

translation: You who slander Layla, can you not see
to whom you carry tales of her, and about whom?
65.sharh: He turns on the talebearer: does he not see that he is bringing his gossip to her lover, and about the woman he loves? No slander can reach a heart already given.

translation: If the ones I love have moved camp, Umm Malik,
the love in my heart has not moved.
66.sharh: Layla's people have struck camp and gone, but the love they left behind stays where it was. The same verb of departure is used twice, once for the tribe and once, denied, for his love.

translation: Lord, since You have made Layla all I wish for,
make me lovely in her eyes, as You made her lovely to me.
67.sharh: He prays that God, who made Layla the whole of his desire, will make him as attractive to her as she is to him. It is the plea of line 25 again: love returned in equal measure.

translation: Or else make her hateful to me, and her family too,
for through Layla I have met with disasters.
68.sharh: If God will not make her love him, he asks for the opposite: let him hate her and her family, since loving her has brought him nothing but misfortune. Either love returned or release; anything but this.

translation: For a woman like Layla a man would kill himself,
even though I keep my despair of Layla folded inside me.
69.sharh: Layla is worth dying for, he says, even though he has quietly accepted that he will never have her. Despair has not cooled his love; it has only been folded away inside him.

translation: My two friends, if they withhold Layla, bring
my bier and my shrouds, and pray God to forgive me.
70.sharh: If her family refuses him, he tells his friends to prepare his funeral: the bier, the shrouds, the prayer for the dead man's forgiveness. Without Layla he counts himself already gone.

translation: And if I die of the sickness of love, carry
my greeting to her who is like the light of the sun.
71.sharh: His last request: should love kill him, his friends are to take his greeting to Layla, whom he calls simply the one like sunlight. Even his farewell is addressed to her.

2.1.2-3.meaning: “Like a spear's shadow”: long. Arabs said of something long that it was longer than a spear's shadow.

3.1.1.head: ثَمدين
3.1.1.meaning: Thamdin: a place; also read Thamdayn, “the two small pools”.

3.2.1-2.head: ذات الغَضى
3.2.1-2.meaning: Dhat al-Ghada: “the place of the ghada”, a desert shrub whose embers burn proverbially hot.

4.2.6.head: يَماني
4.2.6.meaning: Yemeni: from the direction of Yemen, that is, the south.

5.2.1.head: عَلياء
5.2.1.meaning: Alya': a high place, a height.

7.1.2.head: لَيلى
7.1.2.meaning: Layl: Layla, the name shortened as Arabic shortens names when calling someone.

8.1.1.head: خَليل
8.1.1.meaning: “My two friends”: poets often address a pair of companions.

9.1.5.meaning: Sababa: the tenderness and heat of longing.

11.1.1-2.meaning: “May God strip”: a curse, God damn.

12.1.5.meaning: Wearing the usda, a small shift worn under the clothes: she was a little girl.

13.2.1.head: أَعلاق
13.2.1.meaning: A'laq: precious things, so called because the heart clings to them; here, his attachment to her.

14.2.1.head: تَواشى
14.2.1.meaning: They carried tales of us to one another, to make trouble.

15.2.2.meaning: Nawa: the place a traveller is bound for; also distance, parting.

15.2.5.head: المَطالي
15.2.5.meaning: Al-Matali: a place that Yaqut puts in the lands of the clan of Abu Bakr ibn Kilab.

16.2.5.head: السَّواري
16.2.5.meaning: Columns, the pillars of a mosque.

20.1.3.meaning: Tayma: an oasis town on the edge of Syria, on the pilgrims' road from Damascus.

20.2.5-6.meaning: “Cast its anchors”: settled in to stay.

22.1.3.head: واشي
22.1.3.meaning: Washi: a talebearer, one who carries tales to make trouble.

22.1.4.head: اليَمامَة
22.1.4.meaning: Al-Yamama: a region in central Arabia.

22.2.3.meaning: Hadramawt: a region in the far south of Arabia.

23.2.6.head: حِبال
23.2.6.meaning: “My ropes”: the ties of love between them.

24.2.2-3.meaning: “Untwisting and twisting”, as of a rope: making a resolve and breaking it.

25.2.2.head: كَفاف
25.2.2.meaning: Kafaf: just enough, neither more nor less.

26.1.3-6.meaning: The star by which travellers find their way at night.

27.2.1.meaning: Suhayl: Canopus, a bright star that rises in the south, called “the Yemeni star”.

29.1.4.meaning: Janub: the wind that blows from the south.

32.2.3.head: الغَرام
32.2.3.meaning: Gharam: love that clings and torments.

33.1.5-6.meaning: Umm Malik, “mother of Malik”: Layla's kunya, as al-Aghani reports from Abu Ubayda and Abu Amr al-Shaybani; Abu Ubayda quotes this line for it, in another wording.

33.2.2.head: فُوَيد
33.2.2.meaning: Diminutive of fawd: the hair of the head above the ears.

36.2.4.meaning: The place of prayer; here, the direction of prayer, towards Mecca.

37.2.1-2.meaning: Jawa: the burning pain of love or grief; “the weight” of it, its full force.

40.1.6.meaning: Al-Aqiq: a valley; Arabia has many valleys by that name.

41.2.3.head: شَرى
41.2.3.meaning: Is sold. The verb can mean both buying and selling.

46.1.4-5.meaning: “The madman of Amir”: Qays ibn al-Mulawwah's byname; Amir is his tribe, Amir ibn Sa'sa'a.

47.1.5.meaning: Huyam: a madness of love; first, a disease that makes camels wander.

48.2.3.meaning: Deadly: that settle a man's fate.

48.2.4.head: الشَّأن
48.2.4.meaning: “And my affair”: leave the fates and me to each other.

49.1.2-4.meaning: “My eye put on the kohl of your eye”: it saw you.

51.2.2.meaning: Nidw: a camel worn thin by travel; here, what is left of him.

54.1.2.head: اِستَغشى
54.1.2.meaning: I cover myself with my garment, as one does to sleep.

55.1.6.meaning: Ruqya: a charm recited against magic or sickness.

58.1.5.meaning: Turn aside and stop a while.

59.1.4.meaning: Nu'man: a valley between Mecca and Taif, also called Nu'man al-Arak.

59.2.1-2.meaning: “How dear to us”: an exclamation of praise.

62.1.3.head: القُمرِيّ
62.1.3.meaning: Qumri: a turtle-dove, a dove with a sweet call.

63.1.3.head: اِستَطرَبَ
63.1.3.meaning: Moved to tarab, the elation that music or grief stirs.

63.2.2.head: أَطلال
63.2.2.meaning: Atlal: the traces left of an abandoned camp.

64.1.2-3.meaning: “Would that my knowing”: I wish I knew.

69.2.7.head: طاوي
69.2.7.meaning: Folding away: keeping a thing hidden inside oneself.

70.2.2.meaning: The bier on which the dead are carried.

71.2.1-3.meaning: “The one like the light of the sun”: Layla.
